ARCHITECTURE RULES — NON-NEGOTIABLE — READ BEFORE RESPONDING
No standalone pages. Every new feature is a module. modules/{name}_module.php registered in kernel/module_registry.php. Accessed via shell.php?module=name. No exceptions unless explicitly told otherwise.
No embedded CSS. All styles go in ui/global.css. Modules return HTML fragments only — no <style> tags, no <head>, no DOCTYPE.
No embedded CSS in prospect.php or ingest.php either. These are the only legitimate standalone exceptions and they link global.css, not embed styles.
shell.php is a router. ?module=name loads one module full-width. No module param shows the Grand Lobby card dashboard. It does not render all modules simultaneously.
Modules return data, not pages. A module returns a string, a UIC array, or an inspector array. Shell renders it. The module never outputs a full HTML page.
global.css is the only stylesheet. Every page that needs styling links /commandcenter/ui/global.css. One file. Everything inherits from it.
module_registry.php is the source of truth. Every module must be registered there. If it's not in the registry, it doesn't exist to the system.
No AI platform UI chrome in entity extraction. The noise filter in entity_extraction_engine.php handles this. Do not regress it.
Context separation is coming. Do not mix LEGAiSEE business data with General/Memory data in any new DB queries. Tag everything with a context when adding new tables or columns.
Plain English always. Every module output must be human-readable sentences, not raw numbers or key/value dumps.

Key Technical Facts to Remember
Global $db is set at boot — kernel_boot.php sets global $db; $db = kernel_db(); So modules can use either $db OR kernel_db() — both work now.
kernel_validate_runtime() — now defined in kernel_boot.php, returns true if DB connected.
renderModule() in shell.php — uses static $loaded[] to prevent double-loading. If a module name appears twice in the wings array, second load shows "Already loaded: {name}".
UIC types supported: artifact, dataset, system, list, grid + generic fallback for all others. Any module returning array with unknown 'type' gets rendered by render_generic().
Module return options:
Return a string → rendered directly
Return array with 'type' key → routed through uic_render()
Return array without 'type' → rendered as key/value exec-panel
Use ob_start()/ob_get_clean() → return HTML string for complex layouts

**Architecture rule learned this session:**
When a module needs to return JSON (AJAX), it CANNOT go through `shell.php` — the `renderModule()` ob_start() buffer traps the response. All JSON endpoints must live in `api/` and be called directly by URL. Pattern: `api/{name}_action.php` or `api/{name}_load.php`.

---

### Infrastructure Strategy — Decisions Made This Session

#### Server Phase Plan

| Phase | Infrastructure | When |
|-------|---------------|------|
| Phase 1 | SureServer shared hosting — current | Now through first 5-10 paying clients |
| Phase 1.5 | VPS upgrade ($40-80/mo) — same codebase, more RAM + storage | When shared server shows strain |
| Phase 2 | Own dedicated server ($150-300/mo) OR physical box ($3-5k one-time) | After consistent revenue |
| Phase 3 | Client-owned "memory appliance" — physical server at client location | Premium upsell product |

**Current shared server is fine for Phase 1.** The bottleneck will be storage (archived client documents), not CPU. GPU not needed until local AI inference — which is not needed while API calls are available.

#### Deployment Model Decision

**Start: Centralized (John's server)**
All clients on one server. Easier to update, maintain, bill, and iterate.

**Upsell: Client-owned appliance (Model B)**
Physical server installed at client location. Client owns data. $5-15k product + annual support contract. Build this after the software is proven. Strong positioning: "You own your intelligence."

**Long-term: Hybrid (Model C)**
Client owns local memory core + vector DB. John provides intelligence layer, dashboards, model routing, updates via cloud. Recurring revenue + data sovereignty. This is probably the eventual winner.

#### Server Sizing for Multiple Clients (John's hardware)

For 20+ clients in Phase 1-2 (business archaeology, document storage, report generation):

```
CPU:     8-16 core (AMD Ryzen 9 or equivalent) — $300-500
RAM:     64GB — $150
Storage: 4-8TB NAS/SSD — $200-400
GPU:     None needed yet (using APIs)
OS:      Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS
Stack:   PHP 8+, MySQL, Nginx, Docker for vector DB
Monthly: $0 if own hardware, $150-300 if rented dedicated
```

A $2-4k physical server handles Phase 1-2 comfortably. Upgrade GPU when local inference begins.

---

### What LEGAiSEE Actually Is — Vision Locked This Session

LEGAiSEE is not a chatbot, not a website tool, not a reporting dashboard.

**LEGAiSEE is a Business Memory Operating System.**

Core value proposition:
- Companies are sitting on "dark data" — buried marketing assets, forgotten strategies, lost operational knowledge, dormant authority signals
- LEGAiSEE excavates, organizes, and makes that intelligence actionable
- Then it stays alive — continuously ingesting new data so the memory never goes dark again

This is defensible because:
- The longitudinal data (client's full business history) cannot be replicated once built
- Human verification layer (Dig Review) means output is trusted, not just generated
- The longer a client stays, the more valuable the system becomes

---

### Technical Components Needed for Ongoing Business Memory Engine

These are the next major build milestones beyond current Phase 1:

#### 1. Vector Database (Phase 2 priority)

**What:** Converts documents/transcripts into numerical embeddings for semantic search.
**Why:** Keyword search finds "marketing" — vector search finds "any document about brand positioning even if it doesn't use that word."
**How to add:**
- Option A: `pgvector` extension for PostgreSQL (free, familiar SQL-like queries)
- Option B: `Qdrant` — free, runs as Docker container on same server, PHP client available
- Option C: Start with OpenAI embeddings API → store vectors in MySQL BLOB column (hacky but works for Phase 1.5)

**Tables needed:**
```sql
embeddings (
    id, source_table, source_id, context,
    model VARCHAR(64),
    vector BLOB,  -- or use pgvector type
    created_at
)
```

#### 2. Embedding Pipeline

**What:** On every ingest, call embedding API and store the vector.
**Why:** Makes every document semantically searchable immediately.
**How:** PHP function `lee_embed($text)` → calls OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` → stores result.
Cost: ~$0.0001 per 1,000 tokens. A 10,000-word document costs $0.001. Negligible.

**Where it hooks in:** `ingest_module.php` after storing to `memory_ingest`. `entity_extraction_engine.php` after extracting entities.

#### 3. Timeline Engine (partially built)

**What:** Tracks how a business changed over time. Not just "what happened" but "when and in what sequence."
**Why:** The timeline itself IS the product for many clients — seeing their business evolution is the insight.
**Status:** `events` table exists but is empty. `time_intelligence_module.php` exists but shows no data.
**What's needed:** Populate events table from ingested artifacts. Detect date references in documents. Auto-tag events with: `marketing_change`, `leadership_change`, `pricing_change`, `branding_pivot`, `operational_change`.

#### 4. Continuous Ingestion Layer (Phase 2)

**What:** System automatically pulls new data without John manually pasting.
**Sources to add:**
- Website snapshot monitor (cron + diff detection)
- Google Business Profile changes
- Social media activity (where API available)
- Review platform monitoring (Google, Yelp, BBB)
- Ad performance exports (manual upload initially, API later)

**How:** PHP cron scripts in `agents/` folder — already exists in architecture. `agent_tick.php` is the scheduled worker.

#### 5. Authority Scoring Engine (already started in prospect.php)

**What:** Scores a business's authority across multiple dimensions.
**Current state:** `prospect.php` has confidence-weighted scoring (28-96 range).
**What's needed:** Break into sub-dimensions:
```
Digital Presence Score    (0-20)
Content & Credibility     (0-20)
Network Strength          (0-20)
Reputation Signals        (0-20)
Consistency & Clarity     (0-20)
TOTAL                     (0-100)
```
Each sub-score should update over time as new data is ingested. A client's score improving over months IS the product working.

#### 6. Client Isolation (in progress)

**Status:** `context` column SQL migration written and delivered this session.
**What's needed after running migration:** Add `WHERE context = 'legaisee'` to all module queries that should only see business data. Add `WHERE context = 'memory'` for AI session queries.

### Key Technical Facts Added This Session

**AJAX through shell.php is broken by design.**
shell.php uses ob_start() in renderModule(). Any module that needs to return JSON must use `api/` endpoint instead. Pattern: JS fetches `/commandcenter/api/{name}.php?action=...` directly. Never `?module=name&action=...`.

**File manager root:** `KERNEL_ROOT` (commandcenter/ directory). Security check in `files_action.php` ensures all paths stay within that root. kernel/ is explicitly protected from deletion.

**Embedding cost estimate:** OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` at $0.02/million tokens. A client with 500 documents averaging 2,000 words each = 1,000,000 tokens = $0.02 total. Negligible.

**Vector DB recommendation for Phase 1.5:** Start with `pgvector` if moving to PostgreSQL, or store OpenAI embedding vectors as JSON in a MySQL column. Not elegant but works. Migrate to Qdrant when vector queries become frequent.

**The business model insight:** The longer a client's data is in LEGAiSEE, the more valuable the system becomes. This creates natural lock-in through accumulated intelligence, not artificial barriers. That's the right kind of moat.

## CRITICAL: READ THIS BEFORE RESPONDING TO ANYTHING

You are working on LEGAiSEE — a Business Memory Operating System built in PHP on a shared server. Before you write a single line of code or make any suggestion, you must understand and follow every rule in this document. Do not guess. Do not suggest alternatives to the established patterns. Do not introduce new patterns without being asked. The architecture is intentional and must be respected exactly.

---

## ARCHITECTURE RULES — NON-NEGOTIABLE

1. **No standalone pages.** Every new feature is a module. Location: `modules/{name}_module.php`. Registered in `kernel/module_registry.php`. Accessed via `shell.php?module=name`. No exceptions unless explicitly told otherwise by John.

2. **No embedded CSS.** All styles go in `ui/global.css`. Modules return HTML fragments only — no `<style>` tags, no `<head>`, no `<body>`, no `<!DOCTYPE>`.

3. **No embedded CSS in prospect.php or ingest.php either.** These are the only two legitimate standalone exceptions. They link `global.css`, they do not embed styles.

4. **shell.php is a router only.** `?module=name` loads one module full-width. No module param shows the Grand Lobby card dashboard. It does not render all modules simultaneously.

5. **Modules return fragments, not pages.** A module returns a string (via `ob_start()`/`ob_get_clean()`), a UIC array, or an inspector array. Shell renders it. The module never outputs a full HTML page structure.

6. **global.css is the only stylesheet.** Every page that needs styling links `/commandcenter/ui/global.css`. One file. Everything inherits from it.

7. **module_registry.php is the source of truth.** Every module must be registered there. If it's not in the registry, it doesn't exist to the system.

8. **AJAX cannot go through shell.php.** The `renderModule()` function uses `ob_start()` which traps JSON responses in a buffer. Any module needing to return JSON must use a standalone endpoint in `api/`. Pattern: `api/{name}_action.php` or `api/{name}_load.php`. These files require kernel_boot.php directly and bypass shell entirely.

9. **DB access via kernel_db() only.** Never raw PDO inline. Never `global $pdo`. Use `$db = kernel_db();` at the top of every module and engine.

10. **No AI platform UI chrome in entity extraction.** The noise filter in `entity_extraction_engine.php` handles this. Do not regress it.

11. **Context separation is active.** The `context` column exists on all major tables. Values: `legaisee` (business data), `memory` (AI chat sessions), `general` (everything else). Tag everything. Never mix contexts in queries.

12. **Plain English always.** Every module output must be human-readable sentences, not raw numbers or key/value dumps. Use `plain_english_helper.php` in `engine/`.

13. **No form tags in React/artifact code.** Use onClick/onChange event handlers. (Only relevant if building UI artifacts.)

## MODULE PATTERN — EXACT TEMPLATE

Every module must follow this exact pattern:

```php
<?php
// modules/example_module.php

if (!defined('KERNEL_ROOT')) {
    die('Direct access not permitted.');
}

$db = kernel_db();

// ... logic here ...

ob_start();
?>
<!-- HTML fragment here — no DOCTYPE, no head, no body, no style tags -->
<div class="example-wrap">
    <!-- content -->
</div>
<?php
return ob_get_clean();
```

**Module return options:**
- Return a string → rendered directly by shell
- Return array with `'type'` key → routed through `uic_render()`
- `ob_start()`/`ob_get_clean()` → return HTML string (preferred for complex layouts)

**Flow:**
1. Excavation extracts entities/relationships → stored in `entities`/`relationships` tables
2. Click "Queue New Findings" → unreviewed items pulled into `review_flags` with status `pending`
3. John reviews each finding: `confirmed` / `rejected` / `needs_more_info`
4. Report assembly queries only `confirmed` findings

**Schema:**
```sql
review_flags (
    id, source_table, source_id, context,
    status ENUM('pending','confirmed','rejected','needs_more_info'),
    operator_note TEXT,
    reviewed_at DATETIME,
    created_at DATETIME
)
```

**NEEDED:** Add `case_id` column to `review_flags` — required for report assembly to tie findings to specific clients.

## INFRASTRUCTURE ROADMAP

### Current: SureServer shared hosting
Fine for Phase 1. Adequate for ingest, metadata extraction, dashboarding, search, report generation.

### Next upgrade: VPS ($40-80/month)
When: first 5-10 paying clients. Same codebase, more RAM + storage.

### Phase 2: Own dedicated server or physical box
Hardware spec for 20+ clients:
- CPU: 8-16 core
- RAM: 64GB
- Storage: 4-8TB
- GPU: none needed until local AI inference
- Cost: ~$3-5k one-time or $150-300/month rented

### Phase 3 product: Client-owned "memory appliance"
Physical server installed at client location. Client owns data. $5-15k product + annual support.

### Deployment model decision
- Now: Centralized (all clients on John's server) — easier to update/bill
- Premium upsell: Client-owned appliance (data sovereignty)
- Long-term: Hybrid (local memory core + cloud intelligence layer)

## UPCOMING TECHNICAL COMPONENTS (Phase 2)

### Vector Database
Semantic search — finds meaning, not just keywords.
Options: pgvector (PostgreSQL), Qdrant (Docker, free), or store OpenAI vectors as MySQL BLOB.
Cost: OpenAI `text-embedding-3-small` at ~$0.02/million tokens. Negligible.

### Embedding Pipeline
On every ingest: call embedding API → store vector → enables semantic search.
Function needed: `lee_embed($text)` → returns vector → stored in `embeddings` table.

### Timeline Engine
`events` table exists but empty. Needs: date extraction from documents → auto-create events tagged with type (marketing_change, leadership_change, pricing_change, branding_pivot, operational_change).

### Continuous Ingestion
`agents/agent_tick.php` is the cron worker. Phase 2 sources: website snapshots, review platform monitoring, social metrics, ad performance exports.

## KEY TECHNICAL FACTS

- `global $db` is set at boot — `kernel_boot.php` sets `global $db; $db = kernel_db();`. Modules can use either `$db` or `kernel_db()` — both work.
- `kernel_validate_runtime()` returns true if DB connected.
- `renderModule()` uses static `$loaded[]` — second load of same module shows "Already loaded: {name}".
- UIC types: `artifact`, `dataset`, `system`, `list`, `grid` + generic fallback.
- AJAX from modules MUST go to `api/` endpoints — never through `shell.php`.
- `load_json_dir()` in `modules/utils/bootstrap.php` — used by cases, clients, dashboard, insight modules.
- `data/prospects/` auto-created by `prospect.php` on first run.
- DB credentials plaintext in `kernel/kernel_boot.php` — move before portal launch.
- All modules must be registered in `module_registry.php` or they don't exist to the system.
- CSS class naming convention: prefix with module name (`.ingest-wrap`, `.srch3-col`, `.fm-tree-col`).

## 1. BUSINESS IDENTITY

Forensic business archaeology and authority positioning practice. Not marketing. Not strategy consulting. Not content creation. The excavation of what a business has already proved — organised into a signal that commands attention.

**The methodology in one sentence:**  
We don’t find your history. We turn it into Unavoidable Logic.

**The practitioner in one sentence:**  
The forensic discipline of an archivist with the DNA of a master broadcaster.

## 2. DESIGN SYSTEM

### Colour Palette

```
--obsidian:    #050505   (page background)
--surface:     #181818   (darkest section bg)
--card:        #141414   (card background)
--gold:        #C9A961   (primary accent, all gold)
--gold-dim:    rgba(201, 169, 97, 0.32)
--gold-low:    rgba(201, 169, 97, 0.12)
--gold-glow:   rgba(201, 169, 97, 0.08)
--text-primary: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.92)
--text-body:    rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.72)
--text-muted:   rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.45)
```

**NO VIOLET. Ever.**

### Typography

```
--font-display: 'Cinzel Decorative', serif   (headings, h1-h6, display)
--font-body:    'Inter', sans-serif           (body, UI, labels, everything else)
```

**Google Fonts link (correct, confirmed):**

```html
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Cinzel+Decorative:wght@400;700&family=Inter:wght@300;400;500;600&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
```

**NOTE:** Previous sessions used Cinzel + Cormorant Garamond. Those have been superseded. Cinzel Decorative + Inter is the confirmed final font system. All patch CSS references Cormorant Garamond — these are overridden by legaisee-global-fixes.css font declarations.

### Font Size Scale

```
html base:     17px (desktop) / 16px (tablet) / 15.5px (mobile)
h1:            clamp(1.8rem, 5vw, 3.4rem)
h2:            clamp(1.4rem, 3.5vw, 2.4rem)
h3:            clamp(1rem, 2vw, 1.3rem)
.section-title: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 2.6rem)
.section-lead:  clamp(1.05rem, 2vw, 1.25rem) · weight 300
p:             1.05rem · line-height 1.8
body:          1rem · line-height 1.75
UI labels:     0.65–0.7rem · weight 500 · letter-spacing 0.2em
```

### Nav Height

```
--nav-height:    72px (desktop)
--nav-height-sm: 60px (mobile ≤768px)
```

### Card System

Three card types — all separate text from background images:

```
.card-text   — background: #141414, border: rgba(201,169,97,0.13), padding
.card-photo  — background: #141414, no padding, img fills to edges
.card-glass  — background: rgba(14,14,14,0.68), backdrop-filter: blur(18px)
```

Modifiers:

```
.card-text--accented  — 2px gold top border
.card-glass--accented — 2px gold top border
```

Grid layouts:

```
.card-row               — base grid
.card-row--2col         — 1fr 1fr
.card-row--3col         — 1fr 1fr 1fr
.card-row--text-photo   — 1fr 1fr
.card-row--wide-text    — 3fr 2fr
```

All collapse to 1fr on ≤900px.

### Track Lighting System

Museum-style radial gold gradient overlays. Usage:

```html
<section class="section-lit">
  <div class="lighting-overlay"></div>
  <div class="container">
    <!-- content here, z-index: 1 -->
  </div>
</section>
```

Five light positions baked into `.lighting-overlay`:

- A: top centre (main overhead, 0.11 opacity)
- B: bottom left (floor accent, 0.07)
- C: centre right (side track, 0.06)
- D: top left secondary (0.05)
- E: bottom centre fill (0.04)

### Background Image System

```css
/* Desktop — parallax */
.section-bg--parallax { background-attachment: fixed; }

/* All backgrounds */
.section-bg {
  background-size: cover;
  background-position: center center;
  width: 100%;
}

/* Mobile — parallax disabled (iOS Safari bug) */
@media (max-width: 1024px) {
  background-attachment: scroll !important;
  background-size: cover !important;
}
```

Images live at: `legaisee.com/Images/`

### Section Label Pattern (line — TEXT — line)

```html
<div class="section-label">
  <span class="label-line"></span>
  <span class="label-text">Your Label Here</span>
  <span class="label-line"></span>
</div>
```

### Button System

```
.btn             — base (Inter, 0.7rem, 500, 0.2em tracking, uppercase)
.btn-primary     — gold bg, obsidian text
.btn-secondary   — transparent, gold border, gold text
```

## 8. PRACTITIONER PAGE BRIEF

**Page:** architect.html (currently serves as “The Architect” — methodology page)  
**NOTE:** The practitioner’s own institutional record page may need to be a separate page (e.g., `record.html`) or replace/expand the current architect.html. Decide at build time.

### Three-Anchor Structure

#### Anchor 1: The Signal Era (1992–2006)

*Louisiana. Network television. The foundation.*

The practitioner’s record begins not at a freelance gig or a production house. It begins at a network television affiliate, in 1992, directing live broadcasts under FCC regulation with no second takes. Fourteen years across KPLC NBC and KVHP FOX 29. The craft was learned inside a regulated, high-stakes, real-time environment where what goes out over the air is permanent.

This is where the methodology was born. Not theorised — built, under broadcast conditions.

The Addy Award is the documented proof of excellence from this era.  
Carr Multimedia was founded in November 2000, before leaving broadcast. The decision was deliberate.

#### Anchor 2: The Build (2006–2020)

*Texas. Institutional clients. The depth record.*

Fourteen years of documented client work at institutional scale. Houston Methodist Hospital. Texas Flying Legends Museum. MyCare Medical across three cities simultaneously. Early drone operations. Interactive Video built before most production companies had considered it. Discovery Call pre-qualification system operational before the methodology had a name.

The technical substrate: Sowela Technical Institute electronics and instrumentation training. FCC compliance expertise. IT network management across multiple organisations. The practitioner’s capability is not creative — it is technically grounded and systematically applied.

#### Anchor 3: The Archaeology (2020–present)

*The methodology emerges from the record.*

The COVID pivot is not a crisis response. It is the logical conclusion of 28 years of watching businesses use media incorrectly — spending against fictions, building on assumptions, burying their own proof under opinion.

LEGAiSEE is what happens when someone who spent 14 years controlling what goes out over the air, and another 14 years watching what that signal can build or fail to build for institutions of every size, decides to stop producing content and start excavating the proof that should have been driving it.

The methodology applies broadcast discipline — what commands attention, what is unavoidable, what the audience cannot ignore — to the problem of institutional identity.

### Tone Guidance for Page Copy

- First person is acceptable on this page only. Elsewhere the site is third person.
- No false modesty. The record is what it is.
- No marketing language. Every claim cites its source in the record.
- The page should read as LEGAiSEE’s own Exhibit B applied to itself.
- End with the invitation: the practitioner’s record is open. The question is whether yours is.

- [ ] Add one verified metric to each Case Study (I–IV) to replace hypothetical numbers

### Priority 3 — AI System Integration

- [ ] Design AI-powered registry interview (forensic intake, not a form)
- [ ] Define LEGAiSEE system architecture for the AI layer
- [ ] Seed the intake AI with the Carr Multimedia excavation as training reference
- [ ] Build the intake interface as a React artifact or dedicated page

### Priority 4 — Ongoing

- [ ] Periodic dispatch / published signal (4x/year minimum)
- [ ] Deep excavation: Wayback Machine full timeline, Louisiana DBA records, YouTube/Vimeo archive dating
- [ ] Consider practitioner’s own full Exhibit B as the first documented commission

-----

## 10. LEGAISEE AI SYSTEM INTEGRATION

### Concept

Replace the registry form with an AI-powered forensic intake interview. The principal does not fill out a static form. They enter a conversational interface that conducts a structured forensic interview — surfacing preliminary signals before Phase 0 begins.

### What It Does

1. Conducts structured forensic interview (business history, inflection points, competitive environment)
1. Identifies preliminary signals in real time (potential Golden Era, Abandoned Assets, Competitive Gap)
1. Produces structured pre-brief document — delivered to the practitioner, not the principal
1. Principal receives confirmation of receipt and assessment pending
1. Practitioner receives a structured intake document before Phase 0 starts

### Why It Is Not a Lead Magnet

The output goes to the practitioner. The principal gets nothing to keep. It produces a more qualified Phase 0 brief and a faster, deeper Shallow Dig. It self-selects: principals who won’t engage with a forensic interview won’t survive Phase 0.

### Technical Architecture (concept)

- Frontend: React component or dedicated `intake.html` page
- AI layer: Claude API (claude-sonnet-4-20250514) via Anthropic /v1/messages
- Seed context: Carr Multimedia excavation as reference for what a forensic record contains
- Output: Structured JSON brief → formatted PDF or email to practitioner
- No output stored or delivered to principal

### Secondary Integration

- Exhibit C/E/G retainer clients: AI runs continuous signal scanning
- Practitioner interprets forensic layer on top
- Competitive monitoring automated; strategic judgment remains human

### Seed Context for AI

The Carr Multimedia excavation (Section 7 of this Bible) is the reference case. When the AI asks about inflection points, Golden Era, Abandoned Assets — it is drawing from a pattern it has already seen in the practitioner’s own record. That is the most credible possible training context.

-----

## 11. STRATEGIC NOTES

### What the Site Is Missing (structural gaps, not content)

1. **Practitioner page** — the single biggest trust gap. Largest conversion barrier for cold principals. Closes when architect.html or record.html is built.
1. **Verified case study metrics** — Cases I–IV are strong but read as hypothetical. One real number per case changes how all four are read.
1. **Periodic published signal** — not content marketing. Forensic observations. 4x/year minimum. Demonstrates the practitioner is active.

### The Competitive Gap

Nobody in the business archaeology / forensic positioning space has:

- 33 years of documented operational record
- 22 years of timestamped web presence (Wayback)
- Network broadcast credentials
- A formally adjudicated advertising award
- Early drone certification (pre-regulation)
- Institutional clients at hospital system scale

That combination is structurally unassailable if it is documented and published. It is currently under-documented on the live site.

### The Identity Resolution

Three business identities, all documented, all coherent in progression:

1. **Carr Multimedia Digital Creations** (2000–c.2015) — broadcast practitioner applies craft to independent production. Guitar in the header. “Digital Creations” in the logo.
1. **Carr Multimedia Rockstar Marketing Machine** (c.2015–2024) — the strategic pivot. Video as a business tool. Discovery calls. Content strategy. The musical identity still present (“Rockstardom takes flight \m/”).
1. **LEGAiSEE** (2025–present) — the identity resolution. The music identity suppressed. The broadcast discipline formalized as methodology. The excavation turned on the excavator’s own record first.

Each identity is documented. Each transition is evidenced. That is a stronger institutional record than most 33-year-old businesses possess.

### The Founding Principle (from the archive)

*“A Scout is Trustworthy, Loyal, Helpful, Friendly, Courteous, Kind, Obedient, Cheerful, Thrifty, Brave, Clean and Reverent. Once a Scout, Always a Scout.”*

Published in the official institutional values document. Predates LEGAiSEE by at least a decade. The forensic integrity the methodology demands — no cherry-picking, full record, honesty over convenience — has a documented ethical origin. Use it on the practitioner page.

-----

// Accept JSON input
$data = json_decode(file_get_contents("php://input"), true);

$query  = $data['query'] ?? null;

    echo json_encode([
        "status" => "error",
        "message" => "Missing client or query"
    ]);

// Clean client name
function clean($str) {
    $str = strtolower(trim($str));
    $str = preg_replace('/[^a-z0-9_\-]/', '_', $str);
    return preg_replace('/_+/', '_', $str);
}

$client = clean($client);

// Session ID (timestamp-based)
$session_id = date("Ymd_His");

// Base path
$baseDir = $_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT'] . "/legaisee/clients/";

// Session path
$sessionPath = $baseDir . $client . "/excavations/" . $session_id . "/";

// Create folder structure
$folders = [
    $sessionPath,
    $sessionPath . "raw/",
    $sessionPath . "processed/",
    $sessionPath . "output/"
];

foreach ($folders as $folder) {
    if (!is_dir($folder)) {
        mkdir($folder, 0755, true);
    }
}

// Session metadata
$sessionData = [
    "session_id" => $session_id,
    "client" => $client,
    "query" => $query,
    "status" => "created",
    "created_at" => date("Y-m-d H:i:s"),
    "platforms" => []
];

// Save session.json
file_put_contents(
    $sessionPath . "session.json",
    json_encode($sessionData, JSON_PRETTY_PRINT)
);

// RETURN CONTROL FLOW (IMPORTANT)
echo json_encode([
    "status" => "success",
    "session_id" => $session_id,
    "client" => $client,
    "redirect" => "session.php?session=" . $session_id . "&client=" . $client
]);

?>

Internal content=<?php
require_once "db.php";

/*
======================================================
LEGAiSEE EMBEDDING GENERATOR
- Converts page content → OpenAI vector embeddings
======================================================
*/

// ⚠️ INSERT YOUR OPENAI KEY HERE
$OPENAI_API_KEY = "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE";

// -----------------------------
// FETCH UNEMBEDDED PAGES
// -----------------------------
$stmt = $pdo->query("
    SELECT p.id, p.title, pc.content
    FROM page p
    JOIN page_content pc ON pc.page_id = p.id
    WHERE p.embedding IS NULL
    LIMIT 20
");

$pages = $stmt->fetchAll();

// -----------------------------
// OPENAI EMBEDDING FUNCTION
// -----------------------------
function getEmbedding($text, $key) {

    $data = [
        "input" => $text,
        "model" => "text-embedding-3-small"
    ];

    $ch = curl_init("https://api.openai.com/v1/embeddings");

    curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER, true);
    curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_POST, true);

    curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER, [
        "Content-Type: application/json",
        "Authorization: Bearer " . $key
    ]);

    curl_setopt($ch, CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS, json_encode($data));

    $response = curl_exec($ch);
    curl_close($ch);

    $json = json_decode($response, true);

    return $json['data'][0]['embedding'] ?? null;
}

// -----------------------------
// PROCESS PAGES
// -----------------------------
foreach ($pages as $p) {

    $text = $p['title'] . " " . $p['content'];

    $embedding = getEmbedding($text, $OPENAI_API_KEY);

    if (!$embedding) continue;

    $stmt = $pdo->prepare("
        UPDATE page
        SET embedding = ?
        WHERE id = ?
    ");

    $stmt->execute([
        json_encode($embedding),
        $p['id']
    ]);
}

echo "Embedding Complete: " . count($pages) . " processed.";

-File: intelligence.php 
- load:n
- shell:n
- content:No file specified
-internal= <?php

/*
=====================================================
LEGAiSEE INTELLIGENCE ENGINE v1 (LOCAL)
=====================================================
- No API dependencies
- Rule-based extraction
- Outputs structured JSON next to source file
=====================================================
*/

if (!isset($_GET['file'])) {
    die("No file specified");
}

$baseDir = __DIR__ . "/normalized/";
$file = basename($_GET['file']);

$path = realpath($baseDir . $file);

if (!$path || strpos($path, $baseDir) !== 0 || !file_exists($path)) {
    die("Invalid file");
}

$content = file_get_contents($path);
$lines = explode("\n", strtolower($content));

$insights = [];
$actions = [];
$assets = [];
$entities = [];
$keywords = [];

/*
=====================================================
1. ENTITY DETECTION (basic known taxonomy)
=====================================================
*/

$knownEntities = [
    "chatgpt", "gpt", "claude", "gemini", "kimi",
    "openai", "anthropic", "google"
];

foreach ($knownEntities as $e) {
    if (stripos($content, $e) !== false) {
        $entities[] = $e;
    }
}

/*
=====================================================
2. RULE-BASED SENTENCE CLASSIFICATION
=====================================================
*/

foreach ($lines as $line) {

    $line = trim($line);
    if (strlen($line) < 4) continue;

    // ACTION DETECTION
    if (
        str_contains($line, "need to") ||
        str_contains($line, "should") ||
        str_contains($line, "must") ||
        str_contains($line, "going to") ||
        str_contains($line, "will build") ||
        str_contains($line, "we will")
    ) {
        $actions[] = $line;
    }

    // INSIGHT DETECTION
    if (
        str_contains($line, "problem") ||
        str_contains($line, "issue") ||
        str_contains($line, "bottleneck") ||
        str_contains($line, "confusing") ||
        str_contains($line, "important") ||
        str_contains($line, "realization")
    ) {
        $insights[] = $line;
    }

    // ASSET DETECTION
    if (
        str_contains($line, "template") ||
        str_contains($line, "framework") ||
        str_contains($line, "use this") ||
        str_contains($line, "copy") ||
        str_contains($line, "reusable") ||
        str_contains($line, "system")
    ) {
        $assets[] = $line;
    }

    /*
    =====================================================
    3. KEYWORD EXTRACTION (simple frequency model)
    =====================================================
    */

    $words = preg_split('/\s+/', preg_replace('/[^a-z0-9 ]/', '', $line));

    foreach ($words as $w) {
        if (strlen($w) < 4) continue;

        if (!isset($keywords[$w])) {
            $keywords[$w] = 0;
        }
        $keywords[$w]++;
    }
}

/*
=====================================================
4. SORT KEYWORDS BY FREQUENCY
=====================================================
*/

arsort($keywords);

/*
=====================================================
5. FINAL STRUCTURE
=====================================================
*/

$output = [
    "file" => $file,
    "insights" => array_values(array_unique($insights)),
    "actions" => array_values(array_unique($actions)),
    "assets" => array_values(array_unique($assets)),
    "entities" => array_values(array_unique($entities)),
    "keywords" => array_slice(array_keys($keywords), 0, 30)
];

$jsonFile = $path . ".intelligence.json";

file_put_contents($jsonFile, json_encode($output, JSON_PRETTY_PRINT));

echo "INTELLIGENCE GENERATED FOR: " . $file;

?>

-inteernal = <?php

function extractText($filePath, $ext) {

    $ext = strtolower($ext);

    // =====================
    // TXT / MD (DIRECT)
    // =====================
    if ($ext === "txt" || $ext === "md") {
        return file_get_contents($filePath);
    }

    // =====================
    // PDF (FALLBACK METHOD)
    // =====================
    if ($ext === "pdf") {

        // Try pdftotext if available
        $output = shell_exec("pdftotext " . escapeshellarg($filePath) . " -");

        if ($output && trim($output) !== "") {
            return $output;
        }

        return "[PDF: UNABLE TO EXTRACT TEXT - STORED RAW]";
    }

    // =====================
    // DOCX (ZIP XML PARSE)
    // =====================
    if ($ext === "docx") {

        $zip = new ZipArchive;
        if ($zip->open($filePath) === TRUE) {

            $xml = $zip->getFromName("word/document.xml");
            $zip->close();

            if ($xml) {
                $xml = strip_tags($xml);
                return $xml;
            }
        }

        return "[DOCX: UNABLE TO EXTRACT TEXT]";
    }

    // =====================
    // XLSX (BASIC EXTRACTION)
    // =====================
    if ($ext === "xlsx") {

        $zip = new ZipArchive;
        $text = "";

        if ($zip->open($filePath) === TRUE) {

            $xml = $zip->getFromName("xl/sharedStrings.xml");

            if ($xml) {
                $text = strip_tags($xml);
            }

            $zip->close();
        }

        return $text ?: "[XLSX: BASIC EXTRACTION FAILED]";
    }

    // =====================
    // UNKNOWN FILE TYPE
    // =====================
    return "[UNSUPPORTED FILE TYPE]";
}

function normalizeFile($filePath, $meta = []) {

    $ext = pathinfo($filePath, PATHINFO_EXTENSION);

    $text = extractText($filePath, $ext);

    $hash = md5($filePath . time());

    $baseDir = __DIR__ . "/normalized/";

    $client = $meta['client'] ?? "general";

    $dir = $baseDir . $client . "/";

    if (!is_dir($dir)) {
        mkdir($dir, 0755, true);
    }

    $mdFile = $dir . $hash . ".md";
    $jsonFile = $dir . $hash . ".json";

    file_put_contents($mdFile, $text);

    $metaOut = array_merge($meta, [
        "source_file" => $filePath,
        "type" => $ext,
        "word_count" => str_word_count($text),
        "timestamp" => date("Y-m-d H:i:s"),
        "extracted_from" => "parser"
    ]);

    file_put_contents($jsonFile, json_encode($metaOut, JSON_PRETTY_PRINT));

    return $mdFile;
}

?>

- content:# LEGAiSEE Command Center v1.0

Complete Business Archaeology Platform with Multi-AI Excavation

## Features

âœ… Multi-AI Excavation Interface (4 platforms simultaneously)
âœ… Chat Archive with full-text search
âœ… Real Legaisee logo integration
âœ… SQLite database (no MySQL needed)
âœ… Mobile-responsive design

## Files

- setup.php - System initialization
- index.php - Dashboard with logo
- excavation.php - Multi-AI query launcher
- search.php - Full-text search with clickable results
- view.php - Chat viewer with export
- upload.php - File upload interface
- api.php - Backend API

## Installation

1. Upload all files to your server
2. Visit setup.php
3. Click "Initialize System"
4. Done!

## Logo

The system uses your real Legaisee logo from:
https://www.legaisee.com/Images/Legaisee-sm-300.png

No configuration needed - it loads automatically.

## Next Steps

Configure API keys in settings to enable live Multi-AI queries:
- OpenAI (ChatGPT)
- Anthropic (Claude)
- Google (Gemini)
- Perplexity

Without API keys, the excavation interface works in demo mode.

-Internal=<?php
require_once "db.php";

// LOAD PAGES WITH EMBEDDINGS
$stmt = $pdo->query("
    SELECT id, title, embedding, project, platform
    FROM page
    WHERE embedding IS NOT NULL
");

$pages = $stmt->fetchAll();

function cosine($a, $b) {

    $a = json_decode($a, true);
    $b = json_decode($b, true);

    if (!$a || !$b) return 0;

    $dot = 0;
    $magA = 0;
    $magB = 0;

    for ($i = 0; $i < count($a); $i++) {
        $dot += $a[$i] * $b[$i];
        $magA += $a[$i] * $a[$i];
        $magB += $b[$i] * $b[$i];
    }

    return $dot / (sqrt($magA) * sqrt($magB));
}

$update = $pdo->prepare("UPDATE page SET related_ids = ? WHERE id = ?");

foreach ($pages as $p1) {

    $related = [];

    foreach ($pages as $p2) {

        if ($p1['id'] == $p2['id']) continue;

        $score = cosine($p1['embedding'], $p2['embedding']);

        if ($score > 0.78) {
            $related[$p2['id']] = $score;
        }
    }

    arsort($related);
    $top = array_slice(array_keys($related), 0, 5);

    $update->execute([
        implode(",", $top),
        $p1['id']
    ]);
}

echo "Semantic clustering complete.";

$basePath = $_SERVER['DOCUMENT_ROOT'] . "/legaisee/clients/";

$sessionPath = $basePath . $client . "/excavations/" . $session_id . "/";
$rawPath = $sessionPath . "raw/";

if (!is_dir($rawPath)) {
    die("Raw session data not found.");
}

// Load session metadata
$sessionMetaFile = $sessionPath . "session.json";
$sessionMeta = [];

if (file_exists($sessionMetaFile)) {
    $sessionMeta = json_decode(file_get_contents($sessionMetaFile), true);
}

// Get all files
$files = glob($rawPath . "*.md");

$digGroups = [];

foreach ($files as $file) {

    $name = basename($file);

    // skip metadata artifacts
    if (strpos($name, "metadata") !== false) continue;

    // extract dig + platform
    if (preg_match('/^(\d+)_([a-zA-Z]+)/', $name, $m)) {

        $dig = $m[1];
        $platform = strtoupper($m[2]);

        $content = file_get_contents($file);

        $digGroups[$dig][] = [
            "file" => $name,
            "platform" => $platform,
            "content" => $content
        ];
    }
}

- Internal:<?php
// ========================================
// LEGAiSEE EXCAVATION MODULE (FIXED)
// NO DB INCLUDE HERE
// ========================================
?>


<h1>Excavation Control</h1>


<hr>


<h3>Create Client</h3>
<input type="text" id="clientName" placeholder="Enter Client Name">
<button onclick="createClient()">Create Client</button>


<br><br>


<h3>Select Client</h3>
<select id="clientSelect">
    <option value="">Loading...</option>
</select>


<br><br>


<h3>Create Session</h3>
<input type="text" id="sessionName" placeholder="Session Name">
<button onclick="createSession()">Create Session</button>


<br><br>


<h3>Select Session</h3>
<select id="sessionSelect">
    <option value="">Select Client First</option>
</select>


<br><br><br>


<button onclick="runExcavation()" style="padding:10px 20px; font-size:16px;">
    Run Excavation
</button>


<hr>


<pre id="outputBox" style="background:#111; color:#0f0; padding:15px;"></pre>


<script>


// LOAD CLIENTS
async function loadClients() {
    const res = await fetch('api.php?action=get_clients');
    const data = await res.json();


    const select = document.getElementById('clientSelect');
    select.innerHTML = '<option value="">Select Client</option>';


    data.forEach(client => {
        const opt = document.createElement('option');
        opt.value = client.id;
        opt.textContent = client.name;
        select.appendChild(opt);
    });
}


// CREATE CLIENT
async function createClient() {
    const name = document.getElementById('clientName').value;


    if (!name) {
        alert("Enter client name");
        return;
    }


    await fetch('api.php?action=create_client', {
        method: 'POST',
        body: new URLSearchParams({ name })
    });


    document.getElementById('clientName').value = "";
    loadClients();
}


// LOAD SESSIONS
async function loadSessions() {
    const clientId = document.getElementById('clientSelect').value;


    if (!clientId) return;


    const res = await fetch('api.php?action=get_sessions&client_id=' + clientId);
    const data = await res.json();


    const select = document.getElementById('sessionSelect');
    select.innerHTML = '<option value="">Select Session</option>';


    data.forEach(session => {
        const opt = document.createElement('option');
        opt.value = session.id;
        opt.textContent = session.session_name;
        select.appendChild(opt);
    });
}


// CREATE SESSION
async function createSession() {
    const clientId = document.getElementById('clientSelect').value;
    const sessionName = document.getElementById('sessionName').value;


    if (!clientId || !sessionName) {
        alert("Select client and enter session name");
        return;
    }


    await fetch('api.php?action=create_session', {
        method: 'POST',
        body: new URLSearchParams({
            client_id: clientId,
            session_name: sessionName
        })
    });


    document.getElementById('sessionName').value = "";
    loadSessions();
}


// RUN EXCAVATION
async function runExcavation() {
    const sessionId = document.getElementById('sessionSelect').value;


    if (!sessionId) {
        alert("Select a session first");
        return;
    }


    document.getElementById('outputBox').textContent = "Running...";


    const res = await fetch('excavation_engine.php', {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ session_id: sessionId })
    });


    const data = await res.json();


    document.getElementById('outputBox').textContent = JSON.stringify(data, null, 2);
}


// EVENTS
document.getElementById('clientSelect').addEventListener('change', loadSessions);


// INIT
loadClients();


</script>

- Internal:<?php
/* GRAPH MODULE WITH CLUSTER FILTER UI */
?>


<!-- FILTER BAR -->
<div id="clusterFilters" style="
    padding:10px;
    border:1px solid rgba(245,199,106,0.2);
    border-radius:10px;
    margin-bottom:10px;
    display:flex;
    flex-wrap:wrap;
    gap:8px;
"></div>


<!-- GRAPH -->
<div style="
    width:100%;
    height:650px;
    border:1px solid rgba(245,199,106,0.25);
    border-radius:12px;
    overflow:hidden;
">
    <div id="graph" style="width:100%; height:100%;"></div>
</div>


<script src="https://d3js.org/d3.v7.min.js"></script>


<script>


let activeClusters = new Set();


fetch("/commandcenter/data/graph_data.php")
    .then(res => res.json())
    .then(data => {


        if (data.error) {
            document.getElementById("graph").innerHTML =
                "<div style='color:red;padding:20px;'>Data error</div>";
            return;
        }


        const nodes = data.nodes || [];
        const links = data.links || [];


        if (!nodes.length) {
            document.getElementById("graph").innerHTML =
                "<div style='color:#f5c76a;padding:20px;'>No nodes</div>";
            return;
        }


        buildFilters(nodes);
        renderGraph(nodes, links);
    });


/* =========================
   BUILD FILTER BUTTONS
========================= */
function buildFilters(nodes) {


    const container = document.getElementById("clusterFilters");


    const clusterMap = {};


    nodes.forEach(n => {
        const cid = n.cluster || 0;
        const name = n.cluster_name || "Unlabeled";


        if (!clusterMap[cid]) {
            clusterMap[cid] = name;
            activeClusters.add(cid);
        }
    });


    Object.entries(clusterMap).forEach(([cid, name]) => {


        const btn = document.createElement("div");


        btn.innerText = name;
        btn.dataset.cid = cid;


        btn.style.padding = "6px 10px";
        btn.style.border = "1px solid rgba(245,199,106,0.3)";
        btn.style.borderRadius = "6px";
        btn.style.cursor = "pointer";
        btn.style.fontSize = "12px";
        btn.style.background = "rgba(245,199,106,0.15)";


        btn.onclick = () => {


            if (activeClusters.has(cid)) {
                activeClusters.delete(cid);
                btn.style.opacity = 0.3;
            } else {
                activeClusters.add(cid);
                btn.style.opacity = 1;
            }


            updateVisibility();
        };


        container.appendChild(btn);
    });
}


/* =========================
   GRAPH RENDER
========================= */
function renderGraph(nodes, links) {


    const container = document.getElementById("graph");
    const width = container.offsetWidth || 800;
    const height = container.offsetHeight || 650;


    const svg = d3.select("#graph")
        .append("svg")
        .attr("width", width)
        .attr("height", height);


    const simulation = d3.forceSimulation(nodes)
        .force("link", d3.forceLink(links).id(d => d.id).distance(120))
        .force("charge", d3.forceManyBody().strength(-250))
        .force("center", d3.forceCenter(width / 2, height / 2));


    /* LINKS */
    const link = svg.append("g")
        .selectAll("line")
        .data(links)
        .enter()
        .append("line")
        .style("stroke", "rgba(245,199,106,0.35)")
        .style("stroke-width", d => Math.max(1, d.weight || 1));


    /* NODES */
    const node = svg.append("g")
        .selectAll("circle")
        .data(nodes)
        .enter()
        .append("circle")
        .attr("r", 6)
        .style("fill", d => {
            const colors = [
                "#f5c76a","#8be9fd","#ff79c6",
                "#50fa7b","#bd93f9","#ffb86c"
            ];
            return colors[(d.cluster || 0) % colors.length];
        })
        .style("cursor", "pointer")
        .on("click", (event, d) => {
    window.location = "cluster.php?id=" + d.cluster;
}
        });


    /* LABELS */
    const label = svg.append("g")
        .selectAll("text")
        .data(nodes)
        .enter()
        .append("text")
        .text(d => d.title)
        .style("font-size", "10px")
        .style("fill", "#fff");


    simulation.on("tick", () => {


        link
            .attr("x1", d => d.source.x)
            .attr("y1", d => d.source.y)
            .attr("x2", d => d.target.x)
            .attr("y2", d => d.target.y);


        node
            .attr("cx", d => d.x)
            .attr("cy", d => d.y);


        label
            .attr("x", d => d.x + 8)
            .attr("y", d => d.y + 3);
    });


    /* STORE GLOBAL FOR FILTER */
    window._graph = { node, link, nodes, links };
}


/* =========================
   FILTER LOGIC
========================= */
function updateVisibility() {


    const { node, link, nodes } = window._graph;


    node.style("opacity", d =>
        activeClusters.has(String(d.cluster)) ||
        activeClusters.has(d.cluster) ? 1 : 0.1
    );


    link.style("opacity", d => {
        return (
            activeClusters.has(d.source.cluster) &&
            activeClusters.has(d.target.cluster)
        ) ? 1 : 0.05;
    });
}
.on("click", (event, d) => {
    window.location = "cluster.php?id=" + d.cluster;
})
.on("dblclick", (event, d) => {
    window.location = "view.php?id=" + d.id;
})
</script>

if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] === 'POST') {


    $title    = $_POST['title'] ?? "";
    $client   = $_POST['client'] ?? "";
    $system   = $_POST['system'] ?? "";
    $platform = $_POST['platform'] ?? "";
    $content  = $_POST['content'] ?? "";


    if (!$title || !$system || !$platform || !$content) {
        echo "<p style='color:red;'>Missing required fields</p>";
        return;
    }


    // ==========================
    // SAFE VALUES
    // ==========================
    $safeTitle  = preg_replace('/[^a-zA-Z0-9_\-]/', '_', substr($title,0,50));
    $safeClient = preg_replace('/[^a-zA-Z0-9_\-]/', '_', $client);


    $timestamp = date("Ymd_His");


    // ==========================
    // DIRECTORY ROUTING
    // ==========================
    if ($system === "legaisee") {


        if (!$safeClient) {
            echo "<p style='color:red;'>Client required for Legaisee</p>";
            return;
        }


        $targetDir = $legaiseeDir . $safeClient . "/";


    } else {
        $targetDir = $generalDir;
    }


    if (!is_dir($targetDir)) mkdir($targetDir, 0777, true);


    // ==========================
    // FILE NAME
    // ==========================
    $fileName = "{$timestamp}_{$safeTitle}.txt";
    $filePath = $targetDir . $fileName;


    // ==========================
    // STRUCTURED DATA
    // ==========================
    $data =
"TITLE: {$title}


CLIENT: {$client}


SYSTEM: {$system}


PLATFORM: {$platform}


TIMESTAMP: {$timestamp}


CONTENT:
{$content}
";


    file_put_contents($filePath, $data);


    echo "<p style='color:#00ff99;'>Saved → {$filePath}</p>";
}
?>

- content:Relationships
                                      test title 4-26-26                                                  Legaisee Intelligence System Map_4-23-26                                                  Legaisee Potential                                                  Search Dual Scroll and Dual Find                                                  Test Node B                                                  Test Nod A                                                  Server Buildout 1                                                  Server Buildout 2                            Add Relationship

- Internal:<?php


/* --------------------------
   ENSURE DATABASE ACCESS
--------------------------- */
if (!isset($pdo)) {
    require_once __DIR__ . "/../bootstrap.php";
}


/* --------------------------
   GET CURRENT ID
--------------------------- */
$currentId = $_GET['id'] ?? 0;


/* --------------------------
   SAVE RELATION
--------------------------- */
if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] === 'POST' && isset($_POST['target_id'])) {


    $stmt = $pdo->prepare("
        INSERT INTO page_relations (source_id, target_id, relation_type, weight)
        VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
    ");


    $stmt->execute([
        $currentId,
        $_POST['target_id'],
        $_POST['relation_type'] ?? 'related',
        $_POST['weight'] ?? 1
    ]);
}


/* --------------------------
   LOAD OTHER NODES
--------------------------- */
$nodes = $pdo->prepare("
    SELECT id, title
    FROM page
    WHERE id != ?
    ORDER BY created DESC
    LIMIT 200
");


$nodes->execute([$currentId]);


/* --------------------------
   LOAD RELATIONSHIPS (BI-DIRECTIONAL)
--------------------------- */
$relations = $pdo->prepare("
    SELECT pr.*, p.title as target_title
    FROM page_relations pr
    JOIN page p
        ON p.id = IF(pr.source_id = ?, pr.target_id, pr.source_id)
    WHERE pr.source_id = ? OR pr.target_id = ?
");

Here’s a comprehensive Content Strategy Guide tailored for small to medium-sized business owners. This guide is divided into clear, actionable sections that offer valuable insights while positioning Carr Multimedia as an expert resource.

Content Strategy Guide for Small Business Owners
How to Plan, Create, and Distribute Content that Drives Business Growth

Introduction: Why Content Strategy Matters for Small Businesses
Content marketing isn’t just for big brands. As a small or medium-sized business, you can use content to grow your audience, build trust, and drive more traffic to your business. But random acts of content creation aren’t enough—you need a strategy.
A content strategy is a plan for creating and distributing valuable, relevant content to attract and engage your target audience. This guide will walk you through the steps of developing a successful content strategy that aligns with your business goals.

Step 1: Define Your Goals
Before you create any content, it’s crucial to know why you’re creating it. Your goals will guide every aspect of your content strategy, from what topics to cover to how you’ll measure success.
Key Questions to Ask:
What do I want my content to achieve? (e.g., increase brand awareness, generate leads, educate customers)
What actions do I want my audience to take after engaging with my content? (e.g., signing up for a newsletter, scheduling a consultation, making a purchase)
How does content fit into my overall business goals? (e.g., growing revenue, expanding market share)
Common Content Goals:
Brand Awareness: Increase visibility and make your brand recognizable.
Lead Generation: Attract potential customers through valuable content.
Customer Engagement: Build a community around your brand through ongoing interaction.
Sales Enablement: Use content to educate your audience and move them down the sales funnel.
Customer Loyalty & Retention: Nurture existing customers with helpful content that adds value.

Step 2: Understand Your Audience
Knowing your audience is the cornerstone of effective content marketing. If you don’t know who you’re speaking to, your content will miss the mark. Start by creating buyer personas—fictional representations of your ideal customers based on real data.
Key Questions to Ask:
Who is my ideal customer? (e.g., business owners, marketing managers)
What are their pain points and challenges?
What types of content do they prefer to consume? (e.g., blogs, videos, infographics)
Where do they spend their time online? (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn)
Buyer Persona Template:
Demographics: Age, gender, location, job title, income level
Goals: What do they hope to achieve in their business or personal life?
Challenges: What obstacles or pain points are they trying to overcome?
Preferred Content: What type of content are they more likely to engage with?
Where They Engage: Which platforms do they use most?

Step 3: Perform a Content Audit
If you’ve already been creating content, it’s time to take stock of what you have. A content audit helps you evaluate the performance of your existing content and identify gaps in your strategy.
How to Perform a Content Audit:
List all your existing content: Blog posts, social media updates, videos, eBooks, etc.
Analyze performance: Use tools like Google Analytics, Facebook Insights, or Instagram Analytics to see what content has performed well.
Identify gaps: Are there key topics your audience cares about that you haven’t covered yet?
Repurpose content: Can any of your existing content be updated or repurposed into a different format (e.g., turning a blog post into a video)?

Step 4: Create a Content Plan
With your goals and audience in mind, it’s time to create a content plan. This is a roadmap that outlines what content you’ll create, when you’ll create it, and where it will be published.
Key Elements of a Content Plan:
Content Types: Decide what formats will work best for your audience. Common types include:
Blog posts
Videos
Infographics
Case studies
Podcasts
Social media posts
Topics and Themes: Choose topics that address your audience’s pain points and align with your business goals. Use keyword research tools (like Google Keyword Planner or Ubersuggest) to discover relevant search terms.
Content Calendar: Plan your content over the next 3 to 6 months. Make sure to include a variety of content types and themes, and schedule them based on your audience’s preferences and behavior.
Distribution Channels: Decide where to publish your content. Common channels include:
Social media (Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn)
Your website or blog
Email newsletters
Video platforms (YouTube, Vimeo)

Step 5: Create High-Quality Content
Great content is valuable, relevant, and consistent. Aim to create content that is helpful, solves problems, and engages your audience.
Key Tips for Creating Content:
Value First: Always create content that solves a problem or adds value to your audience’s life or business.
Be Consistent: Whether you're posting weekly or bi-weekly, set a schedule and stick to it.
Brand Voice: Maintain a consistent voice and tone that reflects your brand’s personality.
Visuals Matter: Use high-quality images, infographics, or videos to make your content more engaging.
SEO Best Practices: Use relevant keywords, optimize meta descriptions, and structure your content for search engines.

Step 6: Distribute Your Content
Creating great content is only half the battle. You also need to make sure it reaches your target audience. Choose the right distribution channels based on where your audience spends their time and how they like to consume content.
Common Distribution Channels:
Social Media: Share content across your social platforms, but tailor your approach to each one (e.g., more visuals for Instagram, articles for LinkedIn).
Email Marketing: Build an email list and share your content directly with your subscribers.
Paid Ads: Promote your content through Facebook Ads, Google Ads, or sponsored posts on social media.
Partnerships: Collaborate with influencers, partners, or local businesses to expand your reach.
Content Syndication: Republish your content on platforms like Medium or LinkedIn to reach a broader audience.

Step 7: Measure and Optimize Your Strategy
Content marketing is a long-term game, and success doesn’t happen overnight. Regularly measure the performance of your content and optimize your strategy based on the data.
Key Metrics to Track:
Traffic: How many people are visiting your website or content pages?
Engagement: How many likes, shares, and comments is your content receiving?
Conversions: Are visitors taking the desired actions (e.g., signing up, purchasing)?
SEO Performance: Is your content ranking for the right keywords and driving organic traffic?
Tools for Measuring Success:
Google Analytics: For website traffic and behavior insights.
Social Media Analytics: Facebook Insights, Instagram Analytics, LinkedIn Analytics for platform-specific metrics.
Email Marketing Tools: Track open rates, click-through rates, and conversions from email campaigns.

Conclusion: Putting It All Together
A successful content strategy doesn’t have to be complicated, but it does need to be intentional. By understanding your goals, audience, and the types of content that will resonate most with them, you’ll be able to create a plan that helps your business grow.

10 Video Marketing Tips to Boost Your Business in 2024
Proven Strategies for Small and Medium-Sized Businesses

Introduction: Why Video Marketing is Essential for Your Business
Video marketing is no longer a “nice-to-have” for businesses—it's a necessity. Whether you’re promoting a product, showcasing a service, or engaging with your audience, video is one of the most powerful tools at your disposal. In fact, studies show that 86% of businesses use video as a marketing tool, and it’s proven to generate higher engagement, build trust, and convert viewers into customers.
But creating effective video content requires more than just pressing record. This guide will walk you through 10 actionable video marketing tips that can help you attract more customers, grow your brand, and drive business results.

Tip 1: Know Your Audience
Before you even think about creating a video, you need to know who your audience is. Understanding their needs, preferences, and pain points will guide every aspect of your video marketing strategy.
How to Get Started:
Create Buyer Personas: These fictional profiles represent your ideal customers. Include details like demographics, interests, and challenges.
Analyze Your Existing Audience: Use social media insights, website analytics, and customer surveys to learn more about who is engaging with your content.
Tailor Your Messaging: Once you know your audience, craft your video’s message to address their specific needs and pain points.

Tip 2: Use Storytelling to Engage Your Viewers
People love stories, and storytelling is one of the most powerful ways to capture attention and build an emotional connection with your audience. A well-told story can make your brand more relatable and memorable.
Key Elements of a Great Story:
Characters: Every story needs a relatable character, whether it’s your customer, your team, or even your product.
Conflict: Highlight a problem or challenge that your audience can relate to.
Resolution: Show how your product or service solves that problem and improves their lives.
Example:
Instead of just listing the features of a new product, create a story that shows how a customer used it to solve a real problem. This makes the video more engaging and memorable.

Tip 3: Focus on the First 10 Seconds
The first 10 seconds of your video are critical. Studies show that 20% of viewers will click away from a video within 10 seconds if they aren’t engaged. You need to grab their attention right away.
How to Hook Your Audience:
Start with a Bold Statement or Question: Capture interest with a strong opening line that speaks to your audience’s needs.
Use Eye-Catching Visuals: Show something visually interesting in the first few seconds.
Keep it Short: Avoid lengthy intros—get to the point quickly to keep viewers engaged.

Tip 4: Create Different Types of Videos for Different Goals
There isn’t a one-size-fits-all approach to video marketing. Different types of videos serve different purposes in your marketing funnel. To maximize your results, create a mix of videos that align with your business goals.
Types of Videos to Consider:
Brand Awareness Videos: These tell the story of your brand and introduce your business to new audiences.
Product Demos or Explainer Videos: Use these to show off how your product or service works.
Customer Testimonials: Build trust by letting your satisfied customers tell their success stories.
Educational or How-To Videos: Share valuable knowledge that positions your brand as an expert in your field.
Behind-the-Scenes Videos: Give your audience a peek behind the curtain to build a personal connection.

Tip 5: Optimize Your Videos for SEO
Videos can drive traffic to your website, but only if people can find them. Optimizing your videos for search engines is crucial to getting your content discovered.
Key SEO Optimization Tips:
Use Relevant Keywords: Include target keywords in your video titles, descriptions, and tags to help search engines understand what your video is about.
Write Detailed Video Descriptions: Include a well-written description that explains the content of your video and links to your website.
Use Engaging Thumbnails: Thumbnails are the first thing people see when your video appears in search results. Make sure they are eye-catching and relevant to the content.
Enable Closed Captions: Search engines can crawl closed captions, helping your video rank for keywords used in the dialogue.

Tip 6: Include a Clear Call-to-Action (CTA)
Every video should have a clear call-to-action (CTA) that tells viewers what you want them to do next. Whether it’s subscribing to your channel, visiting your website, or contacting you for more information, make sure your CTA is straightforward and compelling.
How to Craft a Strong CTA:
Be Specific: Instead of just saying “Visit our website,” say “Visit our website today to schedule your free consultation.”
Make It Visible: Include the CTA in the video itself (e.g., text overlay) and in the video description.
Create a Sense of Urgency: Use phrases like “limited time” or “act now” to encourage viewers to take immediate action.

Tip 7: Repurpose Your Video Content
Don’t let your video content live in one place. Repurpose it across different channels to get more value out of each video. This also helps you reach different segments of your audience where they are most active.
Ways to Repurpose Videos:
Social Media Clips: Trim down longer videos into bite-sized clips for platforms like Instagram, Facebook, and TikTok.
Blog Posts: Turn the video script or transcript into a blog post or an article.
Email Campaigns: Embed your video in an email to increase engagement.
Infographics or Slides: Use key points from your video to create visuals for LinkedIn or your website.

Tip 8: Leverage Video Ads to Target Specific Audiences
Paid video ads can be a highly effective way to reach your target audience, especially on platforms like Facebook, YouTube, and Instagram. These platforms offer advanced targeting options to get your video in front of the right people.
Best Practices for Video Ads:
Target Specific Demographics: Use the ad platform’s targeting tools to define your audience based on location, interests, and behavior.
Keep Ads Short: Aim for 15-30 seconds for video ads. Capture attention quickly and get your message across efficiently.
Test Different Versions: Experiment with different video formats, CTAs, and targeting options to see what works best.

Tip 9: Measure Performance and Adjust Your Strategy
To ensure your video marketing efforts are effective, you need to track performance and adjust your strategy accordingly. This allows you to understand what’s working and what needs improvement.
Key Metrics to Track:
Views: How many people are watching your video?
Engagement: Are people liking, sharing, and commenting on your video?
Watch Time: How long are viewers watching your video? Are they staying until the end?
Click-Through Rate (CTR): How many people are clicking on your CTA or visiting your website after watching the video?
Tools to Measure Success:
YouTube Analytics: Get insights into how your videos are performing on YouTube.
Facebook and Instagram Insights: Track engagement and reach on social platforms.
Google Analytics: Measure traffic from videos embedded on your website.

Tip 10: Collaborate with Professionals
While DIY videos can be effective, high-quality professional videos can take your marketing to the next level. Partnering with a professional videographer or video marketing agency ensures your content looks polished and delivers your message clearly.
Benefits of Professional Video Production:
High Production Value: Ensure your videos look professional, with great lighting, sound, and editing.
Creative Direction: Professionals can help you tell a compelling story that aligns with your brand.
Efficiency: Save time and effort by working with experts who can manage the entire process from scriptwriting to post-production.

Conclusion: Take Your Video Marketing to the Next Level
Video marketing is one of the most powerful ways to grow your business in 2024. By following these tips, you can create high-quality video content that engages your audience, builds trust, and drives results. But remember, video marketing is a long-term strategy. Consistency and continuous optimization are key to success.

Instructions to Make the Checklist Interactive on WordPress Using Divi:
Step-by-Step Instructions:
Create a New Page or Post on Your WordPress Website:
Go to your WordPress dashboard.
Click on Pages or Posts and then select Add New.
Activate the Divi Builder:
Once you’ve opened the new page or post, click on the Use Divi Builder button at the top of the page.
Choose Build from Scratch to create a customized layout for your interactive checklist.
Add a Title for the Checklist:
Add a Text Module and enter your title: "The Ultimate Business Photography Checklist."
Customize the font, size, and style according to your brand’s aesthetics.
Create the Interactive Checklist:
Below the title, add another Text Module for each section of your checklist.
You’ll now make the checklist interactive by adding checkboxes that users can click to track their progress.
Add Interactive Checkboxes Using the Divi Toggle Module:
For each checklist item (e.g., “Identify Key Goals”), use a Toggle Module or Accordion Module.
Go to the Divi Module Library, search for Toggle, and add it to your page. You can create multiple toggles for each point in the checklist.
Title each toggle with your checklist item, and add detailed information inside the toggle content area.
For simple checkbox interactivity:
Inside the toggle module's content, manually add HTML code for the checkboxes.
html
Copy code
<label><input type="checkbox"> Identify Key Goals</label><br>
<label><input type="checkbox"> Select a Location</label><br>
<label><input type="checkbox"> Confirm Shoot Date and Time</label>


Customize the Design:
Go into the Design tab of each Toggle Module and adjust settings like fonts, colors, background, and spacing to ensure they fit your branding.
Customize the look of the checkboxes using custom CSS if needed:
In the Advanced tab, enter custom CSS under the “Main Element” section:
css
Copy code
input[type="checkbox"] {
    width: 20px;
    height: 20px;
}


Create Multiple Sections for the Checklist:
Repeat steps 4-6 for each section of your checklist (Pre-Session, Preparing, During, Post-Session, and Bonus Tips).
Use Dividers or Section Breaks to separate the sections for easy navigation.
Make the Checklist Saveable or Printable:
To allow users to print the checklist, add a Print Button. You can add a Button Module and link it to a JavaScript print function:
In the Button Module’s Link URL, paste the following:
javascript
Copy code
javascript:window.print();


Preview and Test:
After completing the design, preview the page to ensure everything looks and works as intended.
Test the interactivity of the checkboxes and toggles to make sure they function properly.
Publish the Page:
Once you’re happy with the layout and interactivity, hit Publish.

Additional Tips for Enhancing the User Experience:
Add a Progress Bar: You can add a progress bar to show users how far they’ve come in completing the checklist. Divi allows you to easily add a Progress Bar Module to any part of your page.
Include a Downloadable Version: Offer a PDF download of the checklist for users who prefer to print and use a physical copy. Add a link to the PDF under the checklist or within a button module.
Add Email Capture: If you’re using the checklist as a lead magnet, include an Email Opt-In Module at the top or bottom of the checklist page to encourage users to subscribe before accessing the full checklist.

By following these steps, you can create a visually appealing, fully interactive checklist using Divi. This "Ultimate Business Photography Checklist" will not only be a valuable resource for your visitors but also help you gather leads and establish Carr Multimedia’s authority in business photography.

What to look for
Look for repeated phrases, because those often reveal the real selling system, not just the polished brand. Also look for changes in service names, pricing language, target audience, geographic focus, visual style, and proof points over time. The biggest insights usually come from comparing what the company said publicly in earlier years against what it says now.
Practical workflow
Start with the shallow prompts on search engines, Google Maps, review sites, and social platforms. Then move to archived pages, PDFs, images, and old event materials to reconstruct the brand timeline. Finally, ask the owner and office team for legacy files, dormant devices, and storage locations where old marketing may still exist.

How has BMB evolved workflows since 2001 founding
Based on the material I could verify, BMB’s workflow evolution since its 2001 founding looks like a shift from founder-led, relationship-based custom building toward a more structured, proof-driven luxury delivery system. The public record suggests the company has kept its core custom-home philosophy intact while adding more formalized communication, showcase homes, and process visibility over time.
Likely stages of evolution
2001 to early growth
BMB likely started with a highly hands-on workflow where the founder stayed close to estimating, client selection, design coordination, and major build decisions. That’s typical for a custom builder in its early years, especially in a relationship-driven market where trust and reputation matter more than scale. The workflow at this stage was probably flexible, informal, and heavily dependent on direct communication.
Growth phase
As the company matured, the workflow likely became more repeatable around preconstruction, client communication, and vendor coordination. The language “we build around yours” implies they learned to standardize the client-experience framework without standardizing the home itself. In other words, the process became more systematized, but the product stayed custom.
Recent phase
By the time of their modern public presence, BMB appears to have added more public proof layers: Parade of Homes entries, testimonial pages, and social/video assets. That usually signals an operation that is no longer just delivering homes, but also documenting delivery as part of the brand. The workflow likely now includes more intentional project storytelling, milestone capture, and post-completion reputation building.
What changed operationally
The biggest likely shift is from implicit knowledge to codified process. Early on, much of the builder’s authority probably came from the founder’s memory and judgment; over time, that has likely been translated into repeatable steps for communication, selections, trade coordination, and client updates. Their public emphasis on family stories, trust, and craftsmanship suggests they preserved the human side while reducing chaos behind the scenes.
Another likely change is that BMB learned to treat finished homes as marketing assets, not just delivery outcomes. Parade of Homes participation is especially important here because it forces the company to package workmanship, design decisions, and brand message into one visible experience. That means the workflow evolved to support both construction delivery and public demonstration.
Delivery authority narrative
The strongest narrative is that BMB moved from “a builder who can make a home” to “a builder who can manage a custom-home journey with confidence.” Their authority seems built on consistency, client communication, and the ability to make complex decisions feel manageable. In operational terms, they likely evolved from a craft-led shop into a process-aware luxury builder that still prizes flexibility.
Best reconstruction
If I had to summarize the workflow evolution in one line, it would be this:
BMB likely began as a founder-led custom builder and matured into a more structured, client-guided delivery operation that uses proof, process, and public showcases to reinforce trust.
That’s the core operational story hiding behind the brand.
BMB operational changes post-2001 from interviews or reports

What I can do is give you the most defensible reconstruction based on the public signals already gathered: BMB appears to have shifted from a founder-led, highly flexible custom-build workflow into a more structured, client-guided delivery process that emphasizes communication, trust, and public proof.
